chunks: "An inertial measurement unit is a package that combines motion sensors so you can track how something moves and how it is oriented.
The usual minimum is a three-axis accelerometer and a three-axis gyroscope, which is a six-axis IMU.
Many add a three-axis magnetometer for heading, making nine axes, sometimes a barometer, and increasingly a small processor that does fusion or gesture detection on-chip.
The trade-offs are what matter when choosing one.
First, noise versus bandwidth versus power: a lower noise density and higher output rate give better tracking but cost milliamps, which matters in a wearable.

Second, drift: gyro bias instability and temperature drift decide how long you can free-run, and that spans from tens of degrees per hour for consumer MEMS to a thousandth of a degree per hour for navigation-grade fibre-optic gyros, at a price difference of 10,000 times or more.
Third, range versus resolution: a bigger full-scale range clips less but gives coarser steps.
Fourth, interface and data rate: a six-axis sample at 1 kilohertz over I2C eats a third of the bus, so I might use SPI.
Fifth, mechanical and magnetic environment: vibration, mounting stress, temperature, and for the magnetometer, nearby currents and steel.
So the question I ask is: how long must the IMU free-run between corrections, how fast does the motion change, and what is the power and cost budget?"
